title: Does a reference mismatch lower motor imagery decoding accuracy through covariance geometry?
short_hypothesis: Why does a reference mismatch between training and test reduce motor imagery decoding accuracy, and is the loss explained by covariance geometry?
Although re-referencing is treated as harmless, a reference mismatch lowers decoding accuracy because it rotates the covariance geometry the decoder was fitted on.
The drop itself is tested against matched-reference calibration accuracy; how far each operator moves the geometry is only estimated.
No table reports how fitted weights meet a rotated covariance, so the drop cannot be computed without running the crossover.

abstract.text: Artifact cleaning in motor imagery decoding is scored against expert labels on shared data, and the reference is treated as a fixed, harmless choice of the pipeline.

Yet expert labels are taken as ground truth although class-correlated artifacts challenge them, and the claim that independent component cleaning removes such artifacts rests on a hedge that has not been tested against a known effect.
While this stays open, a decoding gain cannot be attributed to the signal rather than to how the labels and the reference meet.

We cross the training and the test reference on the same epochs of 109 subjects and read the accuracy drop against matched-reference calibration, after a planted rotation and a geometry-preserving relabelling show that the pipeline sees a known effect.
We also estimate how far each reference operator moves the covariance geometry, with its confidence interval.

If the drop reaches two points with an interval that excludes zero, the loss is geometric and repairable by re-alignment; if it stays below two points, the harmless reading of re-referencing holds for this dataset.
Either outcome tells decoding studies whether the reference must be matched between calibration and use, and gives the size of the shift per operator.
